title: Exploring the Detection of Missing Tissue in Planarian Regeneration
abstract: Animals can heal minor injuries, but severe wounds often result in the production of scar tissue. However, some animals can replace lost tissues in a specialized process called regeneration. Schmidtea mediterranea, a planarian flatworm, is a promising model organism for the study of regeneration due to its extensive repair abilities. Planaria can heal after a wide variety of wounds, but the mechanisms that differentiate between injuries that require simple healing and those that require regeneration remain poorly understood. All injuries activate characteristic transcriptional and cellular responses, but these responses are sustained only if tissue is removed by injury. Therefore, it is likely that some unknown signal either induced by or concomitant with tissue loss activates the sustained “missing tissue response” to promote regeneration. To identify this signal, I screened for factors that activate follistatin, a gene whose expression is sustained after tissue loss and initiates the missing tissue response. After silencing the expression of a set of candidate genes, I assessed the level of follistatin expression after injury. Silencing bmp, smad1, and smad4, three members of the BMP signaling pathway, resulted in a failure to activate wound-induced follistatin expression and regeneration defects. This indicates that BMP signaling, which establishes dorsoventral identity in planaria, is involved in sensing tissue loss. Therefore, I propose that contact between dorsal and ventral tissues during wound closure signals that tissue has been lost. Understanding how planaria sense and respond to tissue damage will contribute to fundamental knowledge about the mechanisms that initiate and promote regeneration.
